newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GRAF FACES WTA INVESTIGATION OVER BANNED APPEARANCE FEES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF FACES WTA INVESTIGATION OVER BANNED APPEARANCE FEES.

text.p: International tennis officials are investigating allegations that Steffi Graf took appearance fees at tournaments -- a banned practice which can result in players being thrown out of the sport for three months.

German public prosecutors involved in the much-publicised tax trial involving Graf's father Peter said on Wednesday that the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) had contacted their office for details of the alleged payments.
"A lawyer representing the WTA in Germany has contacted us by 'phone but we demand requests in writing and we have not had that," Mannheim public prosecutor Hubert Jobski said.
"We will have to look at any request and check it carefully. There are German laws on tax secrecy."

Last September the German Tennis Federation (DTB) admitted at the Peter Graf trial that it had paid the world number one hundreds of thousands of dollars each year for "services and advertising" in connection with DTB-run events in Hamburg and Berlin where Graf has often been the main attraction.
DTB chief Guenter Sanders conceded that the cash, said to be between $150,000 and $270,000 a year between 1990 and 1993, was paid to ensure the tournaments had a big-name attraction.
Under the rules of the WTA, which runs the women's tour, players who accept appearance money are liable to a fine of up to $50,000 and a 90-day ban.

WTA officials at the Australian Open where Graf is presently playing confirmed on Wednesday that the organisation was seeking documents about the allegations but would not say whether they had contacted Graf directly about the matter.
While many smaller events need to pull in big stars to sell tickets, the WTA has banned the payments of appearance money for fear that they damage the players' competitiveness.
A top player could turn up and lose in the first round and still walk away with a lucrative fee.

Legal sources said it was unlikely that any documents would be released to the WTA before the verdict in the Peter Graf trial which is expected on January 24, the eve of the women's final in Melbourne.

Graf, who has managed his daughter's financial affairs since she was a teenager, has been accused of evading more than $12 million in tax on the player's earnings between 1989 and 1993. Prosecutors want him jailed for more than six years.

But the WTA investigation threatens to put extra emotional pressure on Steffi Graf who already faces the possibility of having to play a grand slam final less than 24 hours after hearing her father's fate.

The player, who has always had a close relationship with her father, herself remains under scrutiny in the affair but investigators have said suspicions against her are not as serious as those against Peter Graf.
